docs.title: Chapter 1 Glossary
docs.text: Terms introduced in Chapter 1 — Physics and Math Foundations. See the full site Glossary for terms across all chapters.

docs.title: Algebra
docs.text:
The branch of mathematics dealing with symbolic manipulation of equations, including solving for an unknown variable and working with exponents and ratios.

Example: Rearranging the diode current equation \(I = I_0(e^{V/V_T}-1)\) to solve for \(V\) is an algebra skill applied to a physical law.

docs.title: Boltzmann Constant
docs.text:
A fundamental physical constant, \(k_B = 1.381\times10^{-23}\) J/K, that relates the absolute temperature of a system to the average thermal energy of its particles.

See also: Kinetic Theory of Gases, Thermal Equilibrium.

docs.title: Complex Numbers
docs.text:
Numbers of the form \(a+bi\), with real part \(a\) and imaginary part \(b\) where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\), used to represent oscillations, phase, and quantum-mechanical wavefunctions.

Example: Euler's formula, \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\), rewrites an oscillation as a complex exponential.

docs.title: Coulomb's Law
docs.text:
A physical law stating that the electrostatic force between two point charges is proportional to the product of their magnitudes and inversely proportional to the square of the distance separating them.

Example: Two charges separated by 1 nm exert a measurable attractive or repulsive force depending on whether their signs match.

See also: Electric Field, Electric Charge.

docs.title: Curl
docs.text:
A vector-calculus operator that measures the tendency of a vector field to circulate, or rotate, around a given point.

Example: The curl of a static electric field is always zero, which is why such fields can always be written as the gradient of a potential.

Contrast with: Divergence, Gradient.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
The mathematical operation of finding the instantaneous rate of change of a function with respect to one of its variables.

Example: Differentiating position with respect to time gives velocity.

See also: Partial Derivatives, Integration.

docs.title: Divergence
docs.text:
A vector-calculus operator that measures the net outward flow of a vector field per unit volume at a point, indicating whether the point behaves as a source or a sink.

Example: The divergence of the electric field at a point is proportional to the local electric charge density there.

See also: Gauss's Law, Curl.

docs.title: Electric Charge
docs.text:
A fundamental, conserved property of matter that occurs in two signs and is quantized in integer multiples of the elementary charge, \(e = 1.602\times10^{-19}\) C.

Example: An electron carries charge \(-e\); an ionized donor atom carries charge \(+e\).

docs.title: Electric Field
docs.text:
The force per unit charge that a small positive test charge would experience at a given point in space, created by nearby source charges.

Example: Doubling the distance from a point charge reduces the electric field it produces to one-quarter of its original value.

See also: Coulomb's Law, Electric Potential.

docs.title: Electric Flux
docs.text:
A measure of the total electric field passing through a given surface, computed as the field's component perpendicular to the surface integrated over its area.

See also: Gauss's Law.

docs.title: Electric Potential
docs.text:
The electrostatic potential energy per unit charge at a point in space, commonly called voltage; only differences in potential are physically meaningful.

Example: The 0.7 V forward-bias voltage across a silicon diode is a difference in electric potential.

See also: Electrostatic Potential Energy, Gradient.

docs.title: Electrostatic Potential Energy
docs.text:
The potential energy stored in a configuration of two charges held at a fixed separation, equal to one charge's magnitude times the electric potential created by the other.

Example: Moving two like charges closer together increases their electrostatic potential energy.

See also: Electric Potential, Coulomb's Law.

docs.title: Exponentials and Logarithms
docs.text:
A pair of inverse mathematical functions, \(e^x\) and \(\ln x\), used to describe quantities that grow, decay, or accumulate multiplicatively rather than additively.

Example: Carrier concentration in a semiconductor depends exponentially on energy divided by thermal energy, \(k_BT\).

docs.title: Force
docs.text:
A push or pull that, if unopposed, changes an object's velocity; related to mass and acceleration by Newton's second law, \(\vec{F}=m\vec{a}\).

Example: An electric field exerts a force on a charged carrier equal to the charge times the field, \(\vec{F}=q\vec{E}\).

docs.title: Fundamental Physical Constants
docs.text:
Fixed numerical quantities, such as the elementary charge, the permittivity of free space, and Planck's constant, that appear throughout the equations of physics and do not vary between experiments.

See also: SI Units, Boltzmann Constant.

docs.title: Gauss's Law
docs.text:
A law of electrostatics stating that the total electric flux through any closed surface is proportional to the total electric charge enclosed by that surface.

Example: Gauss's Law lets the electric field inside a uniformly charged depletion region be computed without directly integrating Coulomb's Law.

See also: Electric Flux, Divergence.

docs.title: Gradient
docs.text:
A vector-calculus operator that converts a scalar field into a vector field pointing in the direction of the scalar field's steepest increase.

Example: The electric field is the negative gradient of the electric potential, \(\vec{E}=-\nabla V\).

See also: Divergence, Curl.

docs.title: Integration
docs.text:
The mathematical operation, inverse to differentiation, that computes the accumulated total of a continuously varying quantity or the area under a curve.

Example: Integrating the electric field along a path from infinity to a point gives the electric potential at that point.

See also: Differentiation.

docs.title: Kinetic Theory of Gases
docs.text:
A model that treats a gas as a large collection of particles in constant random motion, whose average kinetic energy depends only on absolute temperature.

Example: Doubling a gas's absolute temperature increases the average kinetic energy of its particles proportionally.

See also: Boltzmann Constant, Thermal Equilibrium.

docs.title: Mechanical Energy
docs.text:
The combined kinetic and potential energy of an object due to its motion and position, conserved in an isolated system with no external forces.

Example: A charged particle accelerating through an electric field converts electrostatic potential energy into kinetic energy.

docs.title: Partial Derivatives
docs.text:
The rate of change of a function of several variables with respect to one variable, computed while holding all other variables constant.

Example: For \(V(x,y,z)=x^2y\), the partial derivative \(\partial V/\partial x = 2xy\) treats \(y\) as fixed.

See also: Gradient, Differentiation.

docs.title: Photon Energy
docs.text:
The energy carried by a single discrete packet of electromagnetic radiation, directly proportional to the radiation's frequency.

Example: A photon of red light (650 nm) carries about 1.9 eV of energy.

docs.title: SI Units
docs.text:
The Système International system of standardized physical units, including the meter, kilogram, second, and ampere, used to express all quantities in this course.

See also: Fundamental Physical Constants.

docs.title: Thermal Equilibrium
docs.text:
A state in which a system has a single, well-defined temperature throughout and experiences no net exchange of energy with its surroundings.

Example: A semiconductor crystal left undisturbed at room temperature, with no applied voltage or light, reaches thermal equilibrium.

See also: Kinetic Theory of Gases.

docs.title: Trigonometry
docs.text:
The branch of mathematics describing the relationships between angles and the sides of triangles, used to model periodic and oscillatory phenomena.

Example: Sines and cosines describe the alternating voltage waveform in an AC circuit.

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text:
Quantities possessing both magnitude and direction, in contrast to scalars, which have magnitude only; combined using operations such as the dot product.

Example: Electric field and force are vectors; electric potential and energy are scalars.

See also: Gradient.

docs.title: Chapter 1 Problems - Physics and Math Foundations
End-of-Chapter Problems: Physics and Math Foundations
docs.text: Work through these problems to reinforce your understanding of the physics and mathematics foundations from Chapter 1.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
Convert \(90^\circ\) to radians.

Show Solution

\(90^\circ \times (\pi/180^\circ) = \pi/2\ \text{rad} \approx 1.571\ \text{rad}\).

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
State Newton's second law and identify the SI unit of each quantity in it.

Show Solution

\(\vec{F}=m\vec{a}\); force in newtons (N), mass in kilograms (kg), acceleration in meters per second squared (m/s²).

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
What is the SI unit of electric potential, and what two quantities define it?

Show Solution

Volt (V); defined as potential energy per unit charge, \(V = U/q\).

docs.title: Problem 4
docs.text:
Write the value of the elementary charge \(e\) in coulombs.

Show Solution

\(e = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}\).

docs.title: Problem 5
docs.text:
Simplify \(e^{3}\cdot e^{-5}\).

Show Solution

\(e^{3}\cdot e^{-5} = e^{3-5} = e^{-2} \approx 0.135\).

docs.title: Problem 6
docs.text:
What is the complex conjugate of \(z = 2-5i\)?

Show Solution

\(z^{*} = 2+5i\).

docs.title: Problem 7
docs.text:
Differentiate \(f(x) = 7x^3\).

Show Solution

\(f'(x) = 21x^2\).

docs.title: Problem 8
docs.text:
State Coulomb's law in words (no equation).

Show Solution

The electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of their magnitudes and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, acting along the line joining them.

docs.title: Problem 9
docs.text:
Two charges of \(+4\) nC and \(+4\) nC are separated by 3 nm. Find the electrostatic force between them.

Show Solution

\(F = (8.99\times10^9)\dfrac{(4\times10^{-9})^2}{(3\times10^{-9})^2} = 1.60\times10^{-2}\ \text{N}\) (repulsive, both positive).

docs.title: Problem 10
docs.text:
A test charge of \(+1.5\times10^{-19}\) C experiences a force of \(6.0\times10^{-15}\) N in an electric field. Find the field magnitude.

Show Solution

\(E = F/q = (6.0\times10^{-15})/(1.5\times10^{-19}) = 4.0\times10^{4}\ \text{V/m}\).

docs.title: Problem 11
docs.text:
Solve \(50 = e^{x/0.05}\) for \(x\).

Show Solution

\(\ln(50) = x/0.05 \Rightarrow x = 0.05\times3.912 = 0.1956\).

docs.title: Problem 12
docs.text:
Find \(\partial f/\partial x\) and \(\partial f/\partial y\) for \(f(x,y) = x^3y^2 + 4y\).

Show Solution

\(\partial f/\partial x = 3x^2y^2\); \(\partial f/\partial y = 2x^3y+4\).

docs.title: Problem 13
docs.text:
Evaluate \(\int_0^{2} 3x^2\,dx\).

Show Solution

\(\int_0^2 3x^2\,dx = \big[x^3\big]_0^2 = 8-0 = 8\).

docs.title: Problem 14
docs.text:
Write \(z = -1 + i\) in polar form.

Show Solution

\(r=\sqrt{(-1)^2+1^2}=\sqrt2\); \(\theta = 135^\circ = 3\pi/4\ \text{rad}\) (second quadrant). So \(z=\sqrt2\,e^{i3\pi/4}\).

docs.title: Problem 15
docs.text:
A Gaussian sphere of radius 1 nm encloses a charge of \(-2e\). Find the total flux through the sphere.

Show Solution

\(\Phi_E = Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0 = (-2\times1.602\times10^{-19})/(8.854\times10^{-12}) = -3.62\times10^{-8}\ \text{V·m}\).

docs.title: Problem 16
docs.text:
Find the photon energy, in eV, corresponding to a wavelength of 1100 nm. Is this photon energy above or below silicon's 1.12 eV band gap?

Show Solution

\(E = hc/\lambda = (6.626\times10^{-34})(2.998\times10^8)/(1100\times10^{-9}) = 1.81\times10^{-19}\ \text{J} = 1.13\ \text{eV}\), just above silicon's 1.12 eV band gap (so this photon would still be absorbed, barely).

docs.title: Problem 17
docs.text:
Given \(V(x,y,z) = 5x^2y - 2z^3\) (volts), find the electric field vector \(\vec{E} = -\nabla V\) at the point \((1,2,1)\) meters.

Show Solution

\(\partial V/\partial x = 10xy\), \(\partial V/\partial y = 5x^2\), \(\partial V/\partial z=-6z^2\). At \((1,2,1)\): \(10(1)(2)=20\), \(5(1)^2=5\), \(-6(1)^2=-6\). So \(\vec{E} = -(20\hat{x}+5\hat{y}-6\hat{z})\ \text{V/m} = -20\hat{x}-5\hat{y}+6\hat{z}\ \text{V/m}\).

docs.title: Problem 18
docs.text:
Derive, starting from Coulomb's law, the expression for the electric potential \(V(r)\) of a point charge \(q\), showing the integration step explicitly.

Show Solution

Starting from \(\vec{E} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2}\hat{r}\), integrate along a radial path from infinity to \(r\): \(V(r) = -\int_\infty^r \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l} = -\int_\infty^r \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r'^2}dr' = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{1}{r'}\right]_\infty^r = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{1}{r}-0\right) = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r}\), matching the boxed formula in the Electric Potential subsection.

docs.title: Problem 19
docs.text:
A particle has average kinetic energy \(\langle KE\rangle = 0.05\) eV. Estimate the temperature in kelvin using the kinetic theory of gases result \(\langle KE\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT\).

Show Solution

\(T = \dfrac{2\langle KE\rangle}{3k_B}\). Converting \(0.05\) eV to joules: \(0.05\times1.602\times10^{-19}=8.01\times10^{-21}\ \text{J}\). \(T = \dfrac{2(8.01\times10^{-21})}{3(1.381\times10^{-23})} \approx 387\ \text{K}\).

docs.title: Problem 20
docs.text:
Compute the divergence of the vector field \(\vec{F} = x^2\hat{x} + y^2\hat{y} + z^2\hat{z}\) and evaluate it at the point \((1,1,1)\).

Show Solution

\(\nabla\cdot\vec{F} = \partial(x^2)/\partial x + \partial(y^2)/\partial y + \partial(z^2)/\partial z = 2x+2y+2z\). At \((1,1,1)\): \(2+2+2=6\).

docs.title: Problem 21
docs.text:
Using Euler's formula, show that \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta}}{2}\).

Show Solution

Euler's formula gives \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\) and \(e^{-i\theta}=\cos\theta-i\sin\theta\). Adding: \(e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta}=2\cos\theta\), so \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta}}{2}\), as required.

docs.title: Chapter 1 Quiz - Physics and Math Foundations
Quiz: Physics and Math Foundations
docs.text:
Test your understanding of the physics and mathematics foundations covered in Chapter 1 with these 20 questions.

Question 1

According to Newton's second law as used in this chapter, how is the net force on an object related to its mass and acceleration?

  1. Force equals mass divided by acceleration
  2. Force equals mass times acceleration
  3. Force equals mass plus acceleration
  4. Force equals acceleration divided by mass
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Newton's second law states \(\vec{F}=m\vec{a}\): the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration. This relationship carries over directly to carriers in a semiconductor, where mass is often replaced by an effective mass \(m^*\).

Concept Tested: Force

Question 2

Which statement correctly describes electric charge as introduced in this chapter?

  1. Charge can take any continuous value, not just multiples of a fixed unit
  2. Charge is only ever positive, never negative
  3. Charge is created and destroyed continuously as carriers move
  4. Charge is quantized in integer multiples of the elementary charge, e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C
Show Answer

Correct Answer: D

Electric charge is a fundamental, conserved property of matter that is quantized: \(q=ne\), where \(e=1.602 imes10^{-19}\) C. Options A and C contradict quantization and conservation of charge; option B ignores that charge comes in both signs.

Concept Tested: Electric Charge

Question 3

How is electric potential (voltage) defined in this chapter?

  1. Potential energy per unit charge
  2. Force per unit charge
  3. Charge per unit energy
  4. Energy per unit time
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Electric potential is defined as \(V=U/q\), potential energy per unit charge. Option B describes the electric field, not potential; options C and D do not match any quantity defined in this chapter.

Concept Tested: Electric Potential

Question 4

What physical role does the Boltzmann constant play, as described in this chapter?

  1. It converts electric field into electric potential
  2. It converts frequency into photon energy
  3. It relates absolute temperature to the average thermal energy of particles
  4. It relates electric charge to electric current
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

The Boltzmann constant, \(k_B=1.381 imes10^{-23}\) J/K, bridges macroscopic temperature and microscopic particle energy, as in \(\langle KE angle = frac{3}{2}k_BT\). Option B describes Planck's constant instead.

Concept Tested: Boltzmann Constant

Question 5

What does the divergence of a vector field measure at a point?

  1. The field's rotational tendency around the point
  2. The net outward flow of the field per unit volume at the point
  3. The direction of steepest increase of a scalar quantity
  4. The magnitude of the field at that exact point only
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Divergence, \( abla\cdot\vec{F}\), measures whether a point behaves as a source (positive divergence) or sink (negative divergence) of the field. Option A describes curl, and option C describes the gradient.

Concept Tested: Divergence

Question 6

Two point charges are separated by distance r. If that distance is tripled while the charges stay the same, what happens to the electrostatic force between them, according to Coulomb's Law?

  1. It becomes 1/3 of its original value
  2. It becomes 3 times its original value
  3. It stays the same
  4. It becomes 1/9 of its original value
Show Answer

Correct Answer: D

Coulomb's Law states \(F \propto 1/r^2\). Tripling \(r\) increases \(r^2\) by a factor of 9, so the force drops to \(1/9\) of its original value. This inverse-square sensitivity is why electrostatic force falls off quickly with distance.

Concept Tested: Coulomb's Law

Question 7

Why is the electric field considered a more general description of electrostatic influence than the electrostatic force from Coulomb's Law?

  1. The electric field is defined independent of any particular test charge, describing a property of space itself
  2. The electric field only exists between two specific point charges
  3. The electric field depends on the mass of the source charge
  4. The electric field is a scalar quantity, unlike force
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Unlike Coulomb's Law, which describes force between two specific charges, the electric field \(\vec{E}\) is defined without reference to any particular test charge, making it a property of space created by the source charge(s). It is a vector quantity, not a scalar, so option D is incorrect.

Concept Tested: Electric Field

Question 8

According to Euler's formula introduced in this chapter, how is the complex exponential e^(iθ) related to trigonometric functions?

  1. e^(iθ) equals sin θ divided by cos θ
  2. e^(iθ) equals cos θ plus i sin θ
  3. e^(iθ) equals cos θ minus sin θ
  4. e^(iθ) equals the magnitude of a complex number only
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Euler's formula states \(e^{i heta}=\cos heta + i\sin heta\), connecting complex exponentials to trigonometric functions. This is the identity behind writing traveling waves as complex exponentials in later chapters.

Concept Tested: Complex Numbers

Question 9

How does the electric field relate to the electric potential via the gradient, as presented in this chapter?

  1. The electric field equals the positive gradient of the potential
  2. The electric field equals the curl of the potential
  3. The electric field equals the negative gradient of the potential
  4. The electric field equals the divergence of the potential
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

The chapter states \(\vec{E}=- abla V\): the electric field is the negative gradient of the potential, pointing from high potential toward low potential. Curl and divergence are different operators with different physical meanings.

Concept Tested: Gradient

Question 10

A photon's wavelength is decreased while the speed of light stays constant. Based on E = hc/λ, what happens to its energy?

  1. The photon's energy decreases
  2. The photon's energy stays exactly the same
  3. The photon's energy becomes zero
  4. The photon's energy increases
Show Answer

Correct Answer: D

Since \(E_{ ext{photon}}=hc/\lambda\), energy is inversely proportional to wavelength. Decreasing \(\lambda\) therefore increases the photon's energy — shorter-wavelength light carries more energy per photon.

Concept Tested: Photon Energy

Question 11

Given the potential V(x,y,z) = 3x²y + 2z, what is ∂V/∂x?

  1. 6xy
  2. 3x²
  3. 6x
  4. 3y²
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Treating \(y\) and \(z\) as constants and differentiating \(3x^2y\) with respect to \(x\) gives \(6xy\); the term \(2z\) has no \(x\)-dependence and drops out. This is the same partial-derivative technique used to compute a gradient.

Concept Tested: Partial Derivatives

Question 12

A spherical Gaussian surface encloses a fixed point charge. If the radius of the sphere is doubled while the enclosed charge stays the same, what does Gauss's Law say happens to the total electric flux through the surface?

  1. The flux quadruples
  2. The flux is cut in half
  3. The flux stays exactly the same
  4. The flux drops to zero
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

Gauss's Law, \(\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}=Q_{ ext{enc}}/\varepsilon_0\), shows flux depends only on the enclosed charge, which is unchanged. The electric field magnitude does decrease, but the larger surface area exactly compensates, keeping flux constant.

Concept Tested: Gauss's Law

Question 13

In this chapter's notation, what distinguishes a vector quantity like force from a scalar quantity like energy?

  1. A vector has both magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only
  2. A vector is always negative; a scalar is always positive
  3. A vector can only describe electric quantities; a scalar cannot
  4. A vector has magnitude only; a scalar has both magnitude and direction
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Vectors, such as force and electric field, have both magnitude and direction. Scalars, such as energy and electric potential, have magnitude only. Option D reverses this distinction.

Concept Tested: Vectors

Question 14

What does the curl of the static electric field equal, according to this chapter?

  1. The charge density divided by permittivity
  2. The electric flux through a closed surface
  3. The gradient of the electric potential
  4. Zero
Show Answer

Correct Answer: D

For the electric field produced by static charges, \( abla imes\vec{E}=0\). This is what allows an electrostatic field to always be written as the gradient of a scalar potential.

Concept Tested: Curl

Question 15

How is electric flux through a flat surface in a uniform field defined in this chapter?

  1. The charge enclosed divided by the surface area
  2. The field's component perpendicular to the surface, multiplied by the area
  3. The field's component parallel to the surface, multiplied by the area
  4. The total charge on the surface
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Electric flux is defined as \(\Phi_E = \vec{E}\cdot\vec{A} = EA\cos heta\), the component of the field perpendicular to the surface times the surface area. The parallel component (option C) contributes nothing to flux.

Concept Tested: Electric Flux

Question 16

Why is the permittivity of free space, ε₀, classified as a fundamental physical constant rather than a property specific to one experiment?

  1. Because its value changes depending on which material is being tested
  2. Because it is measured in volts rather than farads per meter
  3. Because it is the same fixed numerical value in every calculation involving electrostatics in a vacuum
  4. Because it only applies inside semiconductor crystals
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

Fundamental physical constants, like \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 imes10^{-12}\) F/m, are fixed numerical quantities that appear throughout physics and do not vary between experiments or materials, unlike measured properties such as doping concentration.

Concept Tested: Fundamental Physical Constants

Question 17

A crystal has a uniform temperature and exchanges no net energy with its surroundings, but a second sample of the same material has hot and cold regions. Which sample is in thermal equilibrium, and why?

  1. The first sample, because it has a single well-defined temperature and no net energy exchange with its surroundings
  2. The second sample, because temperature differences drive useful energy flow
  3. Neither sample, because thermal equilibrium requires an applied voltage
  4. Both samples, because thermal equilibrium only depends on total energy, not its distribution
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Thermal equilibrium requires a single, well-defined temperature throughout the system and no net energy exchange with its surroundings. A sample with hot and cold regions has not reached this state, regardless of its total energy.

Concept Tested: Thermal Equilibrium

Question 18

If two like-signed point charges are moved closer together, what happens to their electrostatic potential energy, based on U = q_test V(r)?

  1. It decreases
  2. It becomes negative
  3. It remains exactly zero
  4. It increases
Show Answer

Correct Answer: D

Since \(U= frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} frac{qq_{ ext{test}}}{r}\) and both charges share a sign, \(U\) is positive and grows larger as \(r\) decreases. It takes work to push like charges closer together.

Concept Tested: Electrostatic Potential Energy

Question 19

Using V = V_T ln(I/I₀ + 1), find V (in volts) when I = 99 I₀ and V_T = 0.0259 V.

  1. 0.0259 V
  2. 0.119 V
  3. 2.59 V
  4. 9.9 V
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Substituting: \(V = 0.0259\ln(99+1) = 0.0259\ln(100) = 0.0259 imes4.605 \approx 0.119\) V. This mirrors the algebra used to solve the diode equation for voltage given current.

Concept Tested: Exponentials and Logarithms

Question 20

A charged particle is released from rest near a fixed point charge of the same sign and moves away under the resulting repulsive force. Which statement best explains the underlying reason its kinetic energy increases while its electrostatic potential energy decreases?

  1. Total charge is being converted into mass as the particle moves
  2. The particle is gaining energy from an external battery not described in the scenario
  3. Conservation of mechanical energy requires that a decrease in potential energy appear as an equal increase in kinetic energy, since no external force removes energy from the system
  4. Kinetic and potential energy are independent quantities with no required relationship
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

In an isolated system, mechanical energy (kinetic plus potential) is conserved. As the particle moves away and its electrostatic potential energy drops, that same amount of energy must appear as kinetic energy — the two are not independent, ruling out option D.

Concept Tested: Mechanical Energy

docs.title: Learning Graph for Semiconductor Physics
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts

This course has 218 concepts spanning prerequisite mathematics and electromagnetics, crystal structure, quantum mechanics and band theory, carrier statistics and transport, the p-n junction, and semiconductor devices. Concepts 201–218 (algebra, trigonometry, complex numbers, differentiation, integration, partial derivatives, vectors, gradient, divergence, curl, electric flux, Gauss's Law, SI units, and fundamental constants) were added after Chapter 1 was written, to represent the prerequisite mathematics and electromagnetics it actually teaches. They were appended with new IDs rather than inserted at the front, so that every original concept ID (1–200) is preserved.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

This taxonomy organizes the 218 concepts in the Semiconductor Physics learning graph into 12 categories, each evenly distributed to avoid any single category dominating the graph.

Category TaxonomyID Description Physics & Math Foundations FOUND Prerequisite physics, mathematics, and quantum mechanics concepts (mechanics, electrostatics, algebra, trigonometry, complex numbers, calculus, vector calculus, Gauss's Law, thermal physics, wave-particle duality, the Schrödinger equation) that underlie the rest of the course. Crystal Structure & Bonding CRYS Crystalline solids: lattice types, unit cells, Miller indices, and the bonding that holds semiconductor crystals together. Quantum Mechanics & Band Theory QMBT How periodic crystal potentials give rise to energy bands, band gaps, and the E-k relationships that distinguish metals, insulators, and semiconductors. Semiconductor Materials & Doping MATL Intrinsic vs. extrinsic materials, donor/acceptor doping, ionization, and the temperature regimes of doped semiconductors. Carrier Statistics STAT Fermi-Dirac statistics, density of states, and the equations governing electron and hole concentrations at equilibrium. Carrier Transport TRAN Drift and diffusion current, mobility, scattering, conductivity, and related transport phenomena (Hall effect, Einstein relation). Non-Equilibrium Carriers NEQ Excess carrier generation and recombination mechanisms, carrier lifetime, and the continuity equation governing non-equilibrium carrier profiles. P-N Junction PNJ The physics of the p-n junction: depletion region, built-in potential, capacitance, the ideal diode equation, and breakdown mechanisms. Metal-Semiconductor Junctions MSJ Schottky barriers, ohmic contacts, and the physics of metal-semiconductor interfaces. MOS Capacitor & Surfaces MOS The MOS capacitor structure, surface conditions (accumulation, depletion, inversion), and threshold voltage — the physical basis of the MOSFET. Optical & Thermal Properties OPT Light absorption, photogeneration, and the optoelectronic and thermal properties of semiconductors. Devices & Applications DEV Applied device concepts (diodes, transistors, device modeling) and the capstone project connecting physics to real device performance.

docs.title: Coulomb's Law Force and Field Explorer
docs.text:
Coulomb's Law Force and Field Explorer

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students adjust two point charges (\(q_1\), \(q_2\)) and their separation (\(r\)) and immediately see the resulting electrostatic force \(F\), the electric field \(E\) and potential \(V\) that \(q_1\) creates at \(q_2\)'s location, and the electrostatic potential energy \(U\) of the pair — all computed from real SI values using \(k=8.99\times10^9\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2\).

Key Features

  • ● Three independent sliders for \(q_1\), \(q_2\) (−5 to +5 nC), and separation \(r\) (0.2 to 5 nm)
  • ● Live numeric readouts of force, field, potential, and energy in scientific notation
  • ● Log-scaled force arrows so both very small and very large forces remain visible on screen
  • ● Reset button returning to the default \(q_1=+2\) nC, \(q_2=-1\) nC, \(r=1\) nm
How to Use
  1. Drag the \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) sliders to change charge magnitude and sign
  2. Drag the \(r\) slider to change separation and watch \(F\) change much faster than \(E\) or \(V\)
  3. Read the numeric panel to see the exact computed values in SI units
  4. Click Reset to return to the default configuration
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply Coulomb's Law to compute the force between two point charges
  • ✓ Apply the point-charge field and potential equations to compute \(E\) and \(V\)
  • ✓ Verify, by direct manipulation, that force falls off faster with distance (\(1/r^2\)) than potential does (\(1/r\))
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the boxed Coulomb's Law, field, and potential equations from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict what happens to \(F\) if \(r\) is doubled
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Set \(q_1=q_2=2\) nC and record \(F\), \(E\), \(V\), \(U\) at \(r=1\) nm
  2. Double \(r\) to 2 nm and compare the new readouts against the prediction (\(F\) should drop to 1/4, \(V\) to 1/2)
  3. Flip the sign of \(q_2\) and observe the arrows reverse direction and \(U\) become negative
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Compare results with Worked Example 9 in the chapter
  • ● Discuss why this distinction matters for the depletion-region field in Chapter 14
References
  • ● Coulomb's Law — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 1: Coulomb's Law — this textbook

docs.text:
Coulomb's Law Force Vectors

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim shows two point charges, \(q_1\) and \(q_2\), drawn along a horizontal line with force vectors indicating the direction of the electrostatic force each charge exerts on the other. Selecting a charge combination toggles between repulsive (like-charge) and attractive (unlike-charge) configurations, and a separation slider shows how the relative force magnitude changes with distance.

Key Features

  • ● Three charge combinations: like-positive, like-negative, and unlike charges
  • ● Force vectors drawn along the line connecting the two charges, pointing apart (repulsion) or together (attraction)
  • ● Separation slider showing the relative force magnitude scale with distance (arrow length shrinks as \(r\) grows)
  • ● Color-coded charges: red for positive, blue for negative
How to Use
  1. Select a charge combination from the dropdown to compare like and unlike charges
  2. Drag the separation slider to see how the force arrows shrink as the charges move apart
  3. Observe the direction of the force vectors and the attractive/repulsive label below the charges
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand (L2)  |  Bloom Verb: Illustrate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Explain that the electrostatic force is a vector directed along the line connecting two point charges
  • ✓ Predict whether a pair of charges will attract or repel based on their signs
  • ✓ Recognize that force magnitude falls off quickly (inverse-square) as separation increases

  • ● Introduce Coulomb's Law in words before showing the equation
  • ● Ask students to predict what happens when two positive charges are brought close together
During the Simulation (5 minutes)
  1. Switch between all three charge combinations and note the arrow directions
  2. Slide the separation control from minimum to maximum and watch the arrows shrink
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect the diagram to the boxed Coulomb's Law equation in the chapter

docs.title: Electric Field and Flux Explorer
docs.text:
Electric Field and Flux Explorer

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim shows the radial electric field of a point charge together with a small flat test surface placed a fixed distance away. A slider tilts the surface's normal vector relative to the field, and a live readout shows the electric field magnitude, the surface area, and the resulting flux \(\Phi_E = EA\cos\theta\) — including the special cases of maximum flux (\(\theta=0°\), normal aligned with the field) and zero flux (\(\theta=90°\), surface parallel to the field).

Key Features

  • ● Charge slider (−5 to +5 nC) that reverses the field direction and the color of the radiating arrows
  • ● Distance slider moving the test surface closer to or farther from the charge
  • ● Angle slider (0–90°) tilting the surface's normal vector relative to the field
  • ● Live numeric readout of \(E\), \(\cos\theta\), and \(\Phi_E\)
How to Use
  1. Set the angle slider to 0° and note the flux is at its maximum (normal aligned with the field)
  2. Slide the angle to 90° and note the flux drops to exactly zero
  3. Change the distance slider and observe that \(E\) changes but \(\Phi_E\) still scales the same way with \(\cos\theta\)
  4. Flip the charge sign to see the field arrows reverse direction
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Compute the electric field of a point charge at a given distance
  • ✓ Apply \(\Phi_E = EA\cos\theta\) to compute electric flux through a flat surface
  • ✓ Explain why flux is maximized when a surface is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel to it
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the definition of electric flux from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict the flux at θ=45°
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Sweep the angle slider from 0° to 90° and record the flux at 0°, 45°, and 90°
  2. Verify the 45° value matches \(E \cdot A \cdot \cos(45°)\) computed by hand
  3. Move the surface closer to the charge and note how much faster \(E\) grows than a linear change
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Preview the next MicroSim (Gauss's Law Explorer), which shows what happens when a surface completely encloses the charge
  • ● Discuss why a solar cell's tilt angle relative to the sun affects the light flux it captures, as a real-world analogy
References
  • ● Electric Flux — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 1: Electric Flux — this textbook

docs.title: Gauss's Law Explorer
docs.text:
Gauss's Law Explorer

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim draws a spherical Gaussian surface (shown as a circle, its 2D cross-section) around a point charge. Changing the surface's radius changes the electric field at the surface, but the total flux \(\Phi_E = Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0\) stays exactly the same, since it depends only on the enclosed charge. A toggle button moves the charge outside the surface, showing that flux drops to exactly zero when no charge is enclosed.

Key Features

  • ● Radius slider (1 to 5 nm) that visibly changes the field strength but not the total flux
  • ● Charge slider (−5 to +5 nC) showing flux scales directly with enclosed charge
  • ● Inside/outside toggle demonstrating that flux is exactly zero when the charge is not enclosed
  • ● Live numeric readout of enclosed charge, field at the surface, and total flux
How to Use
  1. Drag the radius slider and watch the flux readout stay fixed while the field readout changes
  2. Drag the charge slider and watch flux scale directly with the enclosed charge
  3. Click "Move Charge Outside Surface" and note the flux immediately drops to zero, regardless of radius
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, verify

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply Gauss's Law to compute total flux from enclosed charge alone
  • ✓ Verify that flux is independent of the Gaussian surface's size or shape
  • ✓ Explain why charge outside a Gaussian surface contributes zero net flux

  • ● Ask students to predict what happens to flux if the radius is doubled
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Double the radius and confirm the flux readout is unchanged while the field readout drops
  2. Double the charge and confirm the flux readout doubles
  3. Move the charge outside and confirm flux reads exactly zero at every radius
After the Simulation (5 minutes)

docs.text:
Gradient, Divergence, and Curl Explorer

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students switch between the three vector-calculus operators introduced in the chapter — gradient, divergence, and curl — and see each one applied to simple preset fields. In Gradient mode, a colored scalar field (a bowl or a saddle) is overlaid with arrows showing \(\nabla V\), the direction of steepest increase. In Divergence and Curl mode, arrows show a vector field, tinted red/blue (source/sink) or purple (rotational) according to the field's constant analytic divergence or curl.

Key Features

  • ● Operator selector switching between Gradient, Divergence, and Curl
  • ● 2-3 preset fields per operator (bowl/saddle for gradient; source/sink/uniform for divergence; rotational/radial/uniform for curl)
  • ● Quiver-plot arrows at grid points showing field/gradient direction and relative magnitude
  • ● Numeric readout of the exact analytic divergence or curl value for the selected field
How to Use
  1. Choose an operator (Gradient, Divergence, or Curl) from the first dropdown
  2. Choose a preset field from the second dropdown, which updates to show only fields relevant to the selected operator
  3. Compare the arrows and background tint between fields, and read the numeric operator value at the bottom of the canvas
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand (L2)  |  Bloom Verb: Interpret, distinguish

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Distinguish which operator takes a scalar field as input and which take a vector field
  • ✓ Recognize a source field (positive divergence) versus a sink field (negative divergence) versus a divergence-free field
  • ✓ Recognize a rotational field (nonzero curl) versus a curl-free radial or uniform field
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the gradient, divergence, and curl definitions and equations from the chapter
  • ● Ask students which operator they expect to give zero for a uniform field
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. In Gradient mode, compare the bowl and saddle fields and note where the arrows point
  2. In Divergence mode, compare the source and sink fields and note the tint color and sign
  3. In Curl mode, compare the rotational and radial fields and note that only one produces a nonzero curl
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect the "Source (outward)" field to Gauss's Law: positive divergence corresponds to positive charge density
  • ● Note that the radial field's zero curl matches the chapter's statement that static electric fields are curl-free

docs.text:
Maxwell-Boltzmann Speed Distribution

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim plots the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution for a representative gas particle (mass close to an N\(_2\) molecule) as a function of temperature. Dragging the temperature slider shows the curve broaden and its peak shift to higher speed, while numeric readouts show the most probable speed, the RMS speed, and the average kinetic energy \(\langle KE\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT\) in both joules and electron-volts.

Key Features

  • ● Live-updating curve recomputed on every slider change, from 100 K to 1000 K
  • ● Most-probable-speed and RMS-speed markers shown as labeled dashed vertical lines
  • ● Two one-click presets: Room Temperature (300 K) and Liquid Nitrogen (77 K)
  • ● Numeric readout of average kinetic energy in both joules and electron-volts
How to Use
  1. Drag the temperature slider from 100 K to 1000 K and watch the curve broaden and shift right
  2. Click the two preset buttons to directly compare a cryogenic and a room-temperature condition
  3. Read the numeric panel to see how much the average kinetic energy changes between presets
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand (L2)  |  Bloom Verb: Interpret

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Interpret how raising temperature reshapes the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution
  • ✓ Connect the visual broadening of the curve to the increase in \(\langle KE\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT\)
  • ✓ Explain why cooling a device changes the thermal energy available to its carriers
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the kinetic theory of gases and the Boltzmann constant from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict how the curve will change if temperature doubles
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Click Liquid Nitrogen (77 K) and note the narrow, left-shifted curve
  2. Click Room Temperature (300 K) and compare the broader, right-shifted curve
  3. Slide up to 1000 K and observe how far the most-probable-speed line moves
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect back to Worked Example 12 in the chapter
  • ● Preview that this same statistical reasoning reappears for electrons in Chapters 9–10

Photon Energy Across the Electromagnetic Spectrum

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This chart plots photon energy \(E=hc/\lambda\) against wavelength on logarithmic axes spanning gamma rays to radio waves. The visible-light band (380–700 nm) is shaded, and a dashed reference line marks silicon's 1.12 eV band gap, with a marker showing exactly where that energy falls on the curve (near-infrared, about 1107 nm).

Key Features

  • ● Log-log curve computed directly from \(E=hc/\lambda\) across 12 orders of magnitude in wavelength
  • ● Labeled spectrum bands: gamma ray, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, and radio
  • ● Shaded visible-light region and a dashed silicon band-gap reference line
  • ● Hover tooltips showing the exact energy and wavelength at any point on the curve
How to Use
  1. Hover over the curve anywhere to read the exact photon energy and wavelength
  2. Find the shaded visible band and note how narrow it is compared to the full spectrum
  3. Locate the red dot where the silicon band-gap line crosses the curve, just past visible light in the near-infrared
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Analyze (L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Compare

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Compare photon energies across the electromagnetic spectrum
  • ✓ Locate where silicon's band gap falls relative to visible light
  • ✓ Explain why a semiconductor absorbs some wavelengths of light but not others
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the photon energy equation \(E=hc/\lambda\) from the chapter
  • ● Ask students whether higher or lower wavelength means higher photon energy
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Hover over the gamma-ray and radio-wave ends of the curve and compare the energy values
  2. Find the visible-light band and read off the energy range of visible photons
  3. Locate the silicon band-gap marker and discuss why light just past red (near-infrared) can still be absorbed
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect back to Worked Example 11 in the chapter
  • ● Preview optical absorption and solar cells in Chapter 17

docs.title: Vector Components and Addition
docs.text:
Vector Components and Addition

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students build two vectors, \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\), by setting their magnitude and direction angle, and see the resulting x and y components. A tip-to-tail construction shows how the two vectors add to form the resultant \(\vec{R}=\vec{A}+\vec{B}\), with all magnitudes, angles, and components displayed numerically.

Key Features

  • ● Four sliders controlling the magnitude and angle of two independent vectors
  • ● Dashed component projections onto the x and y axes (toggle on/off)
  • ● Tip-to-tail construction showing \(\vec{B}\) redrawn from the tip of \(\vec{A}\) to form the resultant
  • ● Full numeric readout of magnitude, angle, and components for A, B, and R
How to Use
  1. Adjust |A| and θA to change the blue vector's magnitude and direction
  2. Adjust |B| and θB to change the green vector
  3. Watch the red resultant \(\vec{R}\) update as you move either vector
  4. Toggle component projections to see how \(A_x\), \(A_y\) relate to \(|\vec{A}|\) and \(\theta_A\)
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Construct, compute

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Decompose a vector into its x and y components given a magnitude and angle
  • ✓ Add two vectors component-wise and graphically using the tip-to-tail method
  • ✓ Recover the magnitude and direction of a resultant vector from its components
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the definition of a vector versus a scalar from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict the components of a vector at 90° and at 180°
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Set A to magnitude 5 at 0° and read off its components
  2. Set A to magnitude 5 at 90° and compare
  3. Add a second vector B and verify \(R_x = A_x+B_x\) and \(R_y=A_y+B_y\) against the on-screen readout
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect back to the Vectors subsection in the Vector Calculus section of the chapter
  • ● Preview that force and electric field are vectors added the same way
